summary: This unit teaches you to find, read and apply the documents that control fabrication work: standards and codes, job specifications, drawings, welding procedures, material certificates, equipment manuals, data sheets and safety data sheets. You will learn to check that every document is the current issue, to pick out firm requirements, tolerances and acceptance limits, and to settle conflicts and unclear wording through the right people. You will also use manuals and data sheets to set up, maintain and fault-find equipment, plan painting and storage, and brief your team.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Welding Level 3 qualification (MEM30215). At Level 3 you do more than follow instructions: you read the documents behind a job, check that they are current and that they agree with each other, apply their requirements and limits, and explain them to the people you lead.

Every steel job is controlled by paper (or screen) as well as by skill. A stair tower for a hotel, a platform at a water-treatment works or a set of school gates comes with a **specification**, **drawings**, a **welding procedure**, **certificates** for the steel, **data sheets** for the consumables and paint, and the **manuals** for the machines used. A mistake in reading any one of them can mean the wrong steel, the wrong weld size, a weld that fails inspection, or a machine that is damaged or unsafe.
**Who it is for:** Level 3 trainees and welders who lead a small team, plan work, check materials and inspect welds, in a training centre, a fabrication shop or on site.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means in the workshop
rows: Know which standard, specification, drawing, procedure, manual or data sheet controls each part of a job, and get the current issue of each.
Compare revisions with the document register, work only from controlled or approved copies, and withdraw superseded copies.
Pick out the firm requirements ("shall"), the advice ("should"), the tolerances and the acceptance limits, and use the meanings the document itself defines.
Deal with conflicts and unclear wording
Apply the contract's order of priority, raise written queries, and never guess or pick the easier meaning.
Match steel, bolts and consumables to the specification using certificates, markings and data sheets, and keep traceability through cutting and welding.
Work to the welding procedure specification (WPS), use welders qualified for the work, inspect against the acceptance limits and record the results.
Have machines connected by an electrician to the manual's figures, then set up, maintain and fault-find them as the maker says.
Use data sheets, SDS and labels
Plan painting, storage and safe handling from data sheets, safety data sheets (SDS) and product labels.
Turn what the documents require into clear instructions, and check that the team follows them.
Keep query logs, inspection and traceability records, and report errors found in documents.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** on kinds of documents, document control, conflicts, acceptance criteria, materials and certificates, consumables, procedures and qualifications, inspection, manuals, rating plates, data sheets and labels.
A **written paper**: short answers that need exact terms (for example superseded, concession, heat number, essential variables, duty cycle, normative references) and longer answers in full sentences.

**Practical tasks**: reviewing a specification pack with planted problems, checking plates against their certificates and inspecting sample welds with gauges; and setting up, maintaining and fault-finding a MIG machine from its manual, then writing a work instruction.

blocks.note: At Level 3 the examiner wants the reason as well as the answer: why the old revision must go, why the stricter rule wins, why a grade cannot be swapped. Learn the reasons as you read.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Each document on a job has a different author, a different purpose and a different weight. Before you can apply one, you must know what kind it is.

head: Document
Who writes it
What it covers
How binding it is
rows: Standard (for example ISO, BS EN, ASTM, AWS, or a Jamaican Standard)
A standards body, through a committee of experts
General agreed rules: material grades, test methods, weld quality, symbols, safety of equipment
Binding on a job only when a contract, a specification or a law calls it up
Code (for example a structural welding code or a building code)
A standards body or professional society; a building code is made law by the government
A full set of rules for one kind of work, such as welded steel structures or pressure vessels
Binding when the contract or the law names it
The client's engineer or designer, for this one job
What this job must meet: materials, sizes, workmanship, inspection, painting; it names the standards that apply
Shapes, sizes, tolerances, weld symbols, materials list and revision
Binding under the contract, together with the specification
The fabricator, backed by a test (the procedure qualification record)
The exact process, consumables, settings, joint details and temperatures for a weld
Must be followed by the welder for every weld it covers
The maker of a machine, tool or product
Safe installation, use, maintenance, fault-finding and parts
Needed for safe use and to keep the warranty; site rules and safety law expect it to be followed
The maker of a consumable, paint or other product
Properties, settings, mixing, application, storage and limits
Followed as the maker's instructions; the specification often names the product
The maker or supplier of a hazardous product
Hazards, safe handling and storage, PPE, first aid, fire-fighting, spills and disposal
Must be available to users and followed
Steel mill, test house, inspector or calibration laboratory
Proof that materials, welders, procedures and instruments meet requirements
The evidence the job needs; checked before the item or person is used

ul: **International:** ISO (most subjects) and IEC (electrical equipment, including welding power sources).
**European and British:** EN standards, published in the UK as BS EN. Steel grades such as S275 and S355 come from these.
**American:** ASTM (materials such as A36 steel), AWS (welding: codes, consumable classifications, symbols), ASME (boilers, pressure vessels and pipework) and ANSI.
**Jamaican:** the **Bureau of Standards Jamaica (BSJ)** is the national standards body. It publishes Jamaican Standards and adopts many international ones.

blocks.note: Jamaican jobs often name an American or an international standard, because the designer, the client or the money comes from abroad, or because there is no Jamaican standard for that work. The job specification tells you which standards apply. If it does not, ask before work starts; do not choose one yourself.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.h: How the documents for one weld fit together

flow: The specification names the code and the acceptance limits
The code sets the rules for procedures, welders and inspection
The fabricator writes a WPS and proves it with a test weld (PQR)
Each welder is tested and qualified for the work (welder qualification record)
The welder makes the weld to the WPS, with materials that match their certificates
The inspector checks the weld against the acceptance limits and records the result

blocks.p: The higher documents say **what** is required; the lower ones say **how** it will be done. If a lower document (such as a WPS) does not meet a higher one (such as the specification), the lower one must be changed and approved, not ignored.

head: Your question
Where to look first
rows: What grade and size of steel?
The drawing's materials list and the specification
What size and type of weld?
The drawing (weld symbols and notes) and the specification
Which process, electrode or wire, current and preheat?
Is this welder allowed to make this weld?
The welder qualification record, compared with the WPS and position
Is this plate the steel we ordered?
The markings on the steel and its mill certificate
How do I set up, maintain or fix this machine?
The maker's manual: set-up, maintenance and troubleshooting sections
What PPE and ventilation does this thinner need?

blocks.note: A standard is general; a specification is about this job. A WPS tells the welder how to weld; the acceptance criteria say what is good enough. A manual tells you how to use the machine safely.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Standards and specifications follow a set pattern. Once you know the pattern you can find what you need quickly and you will not miss the parts that change its meaning.

head: Part
What it tells you
Why it matters
rows: Title, number, edition or revision, date
You must use the issue the contract names, or else the current one
Background, and what changed from the last edition
Warns you of changes you might not expect
What the document covers and what it does not: processes, materials, thicknesses, kinds of work
Read it first. A standard used outside its scope proves nothing
Other documents that must be used with this one, as if their requirements were written into it
You need those documents too. A dated reference (with a year) means that edition only; an undated one means the latest edition
The exact meaning of words used in the document
The document's own definition wins over shop habit or the dictionary
What must be done, often with figures
Read the units and the notes under each table
Extra material at the back. A **normative** annex is part of the requirements; an **informative** annex is guidance only
Check which kind it is before you rely on it

blocks.h: The words that set the strength of a requirement

head: Word
Meaning
Example
rows: A firm requirement: it must be done
"All welds shall be free of cracks."
"Welding shall not be carried out on wet surfaces."
A recommendation: the expected or preferred way. Another way may be accepted, but only with a good reason and the agreement of the engineer
"Preheat should be checked with temperature-indicating crayons."
"Back gouging may be done by grinding."
Possibility or ability: a statement of fact, not a requirement
"Undercut can be caused by too high a current."

blocks.note: When you brief the team, separate the "shall" requirements from the "should" advice. Treat a "should" as the method to use unless the engineer has agreed another one in writing. Never treat a "shall" as optional because it is inconvenient.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: A **tolerance** is how far a size may vary from the size given. The two ends of the allowed range are the **limits**.

ul: "250 ± 1.5" allows 248.5 to 251.5 mm. A reading exactly on a limit is inside the tolerance.
"60 +0.5 / −0" allows 60.0 to 60.5 mm: the tolerance can be on one side only.

A **general tolerance** note (for example "unless stated otherwise ±2 mm") covers every size that has no tolerance of its own. A tolerance written on a particular size **overrides** the general note for that size.
Tolerances for straightness, squareness and twist apply to the finished item, after welding, so plan for distortion before you weld.
The general tolerance may sit in the title block, in a drawing note, in the specification or in a standard the specification calls up. Find it before you start.

blocks.p: Standards and data sheets from the USA often use inches, feet, pounds, psi, ksi and degrees Fahrenheit. Jamaican drawings are normally metric. **Convert once, write both values down, and have another person check them.** Never let each person convert as they go.

head: Imperial unit
Metric equivalent
rows: about 6.9 kPa (1 bar is about 14.5 psi)

blocks.note: 1 MPa is the same as 1 N/mm². Steel and bolt strengths are given in either unit.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: Read the headings, the units and the notes under the table first.
Find the row and column that fit your job exactly: material, thickness, position, wire or electrode size.
Where the table gives a range, start near the middle and fine-tune on a test piece of the same material and thickness.
If your job falls between two rows, use the rule the table's notes give (often the thicker plate or the safer value). If there is no rule, ask; never invent a value outside the table.
Check that the table comes from the current issue and is for the product you actually have.

blocks.p: A shop can hold the right specification and still get the job wrong if a team works from last month's revision. **Document control** makes sure that everyone works from the current issue, and that changes reach the people who need them.

head: Term
Meaning
rows: A list of every controlled document for a job or a shop: number, title, current revision and date, and who holds a copy
An issue of a document, shown by a letter (A, B, C) or a number (0, 1, 2) with a date. Drawings show what changed with a revision cloud and a line in the revision table
A copy stamped and numbered and issued to a named holder, who is sent each new revision and hands back the old one
A photocopy, printout or download that nobody tracks. It is marked "uncontrolled" or "for information only" and must be checked against the register before it is used
Replaced by a newer revision. It is withdrawn, or kept clearly stamped SUPERSEDED for the record
The form sent with a new revision, listing what is sent; the holder signs to show it was received
Only drawings marked for construction (for example "approved for construction") may be built from. "Preliminary", "for comment" or "for tender" drawings may not

blocks.h: How a new revision is handled

flow: The new revision is issued with a transmittal
The person in charge of documents updates the register
Each named holder receives a copy and signs the transmittal
Old copies are collected and destroyed, or stamped SUPERSEDED; one marked original is kept for the record
The team leader briefs the team on what changed and checks whether work already done is affected

ul: An approved copy on the shop's computer system or tablet can be the controlled version. A photo or PDF passed round on a phone is not.
A printout is uncontrolled from the moment it is printed, unless it is stamped and logged.
Before each job, compare the revision on your copy with the register. It takes a minute and can save a week of rework.

blocks.h: If you find an old copy in use

ol: Stop the work that depends on it.
Compare it with the register and get the current revision.
Find out what changed, and whether any work done to the old copy is affected.
Tell the supervisor and record what happened. Remove the old copy or mark it SUPERSEDED.

blocks.p: If a new revision arrives part-way through a job, work already done to the old revision is not automatically wrong, but it is not automatically accepted either. Stop the affected work, tell the supervisor and get a **written** decision from the engineer or client: change it, carry on, or accept what has been done. A change of this kind may also change the price or the time (a **variation**).

Most contracts give an **order of priority** (order of precedence) that says which document wins when two disagree. One common order is: the contract conditions, then the specification, then the drawings, then the standards called up. Every contract can set its own order, so read yours.

ul: A size written on the drawing beats a size measured off the drawing. **Never scale a drawing** to find a missing size: ask.
A specific note or tolerance beats a general one.
A document may settle the question itself: "6 mm unless a larger size is shown on the drawings" means a larger size on the drawing applies.
For safety rules, the **stricter rule applies**. If the maker's manual asks for safety glasses and the Centre's rule asks for glasses and a face shield, wear both.
Even when the order of priority tells you which document wins, tell the engineer so that the other document is corrected.
If there is no order of priority, or the meaning is unclear, do not choose: raise a query.

flow: Read the whole section again, with the definitions, notes and the other documents
If still unclear, stop only the work that depends on it and tell the supervisor
Write the query: document number and revision, the clause or detail, the exact words, the problem, and a proposed answer if you have one
Enter it in the query log with a number and date, and send it to the engineer or client
Carry on with work the query does not affect
When the written answer comes, file it, mark the register or controlled copy, and brief the team
If the answer changes the cost or time, the supervisor raises a variation

head: Query log column
Example entry
rows: Specification Rev C, welding section; drawing S-104 Rev B
Drawing shows 5 mm fillets on the handrail brackets; specification says "minimum fillet size 6 mm"
Weld 6 mm and correct the drawing (specification has priority in this contract)
Project engineer, 12 March; 6 mm confirmed in writing 13 March; closed by team leader

blocks.h: When work does not meet the specification

head: Term
Meaning
rows: Work, material or a document that does not meet a requirement
The written record of the problem, its cause and what will be done
Putting it right by an approved method, followed by inspection again
Written permission from the client or engineer to accept something, as it is, that does not fully meet the specification
Written permission, given before the work is done, to depart from a requirement
A change to the job agreed with the client, usually with a change in price or time

blocks.note: Only the client or the engineer named in the contract can grant a concession. A welder, a team leader or an inspector cannot "let it go", and a verbal "it's fine" is not a concession.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.h: Reviewing a specification pack before work starts

flow: Check every document listed is present and is the revision in the register
Read the scopes to confirm the documents fit this job, its steel and its process
Read the specification in full and mark the "shall" requirements: materials, weld sizes, acceptance limits, inspection, painting
Cross-check the drawings, WPS, certificates and data sheets against the specification and against each other
Check that the team's qualifications and the shop's equipment can meet the requirements
Log each problem with the documents involved, a proposed action and who should decide
Get written answers before the affected work starts, then brief the team

blocks.p: Problems often found in a pack: an out-of-date revision; a size or grade that differs between drawing and specification; a WPS for a different process, thickness or consumable; a plate whose heat number is not on any certificate; a welder whose qualification does not cover the position; mixed units; a paint system that differs from the specification.
European structural steel grades look like **S355J2** or **S275JR**. Each part means something.

head: Part
Meaning
In S355J2
rows: Minimum **yield strength** in MPa (N/mm²) for the thinner plates (up to 16 mm). Thicker plate has a slightly lower minimum
Impact toughness: tested (Charpy test) at +20 °C for JR, 0 °C for J0 and −20 °C for J2
The delivery condition, such as normalised or as-rolled

ul: Yield strength is the stress at which the steel starts to stretch permanently. Designers work from it, so a lower grade is weaker in use even if it looks the same.
American grades are common in Jamaica too: **ASTM A36** has a minimum yield of 36 ksi (about 250 MPa); **ASTM A572 Grade 50** about 345 MPa.
A lower grade must never replace a higher one. A higher grade may replace a lower one only with the engineer's approval: it may need a different WPS or preheat, and it may bend differently.

blocks.p: A **mill test certificate (MTC)**, also called a mill certificate or inspection certificate, comes from the steel maker. It shows: the maker; the **heat (cast) number**; the grade and the standard it meets; the sizes; the chemical analysis (carbon, manganese, silicon, phosphorus, sulphur and others); the test results (yield and tensile strength, elongation, impact energy); the delivery condition; the type of certificate; and a signature or stamp.

head: Certificate type (EN 10204, used worldwide)
What it gives you
rows: A declaration that the product meets the order. No test results
A test report: results from the maker's routine tests on that kind of product, not on the actual items supplied
An inspection certificate: results of tests on the actual product supplied, signed by the maker's inspection department, which is independent of production
As 3.1, and also signed by the buyer's inspector or an independent third party

blocks.p: The specification says which type is needed. Structural and pressure work usually asks for type 3.1 or 3.2. A lower type than the specification asks for is a non-conformance, even if the steel is the right grade.

flow: Compare the delivery note with the order: grades, sizes and quantities
Find the identification on each piece: heat number, grade and size (stamped, stencilled, painted or on a tag)
Match each piece to its certificate by heat number
Check the certificate values meet the specification: grade, impact temperature, yield strength, thickness, certificate type
Anything without a matching certificate, or with missing or wrong marks, is tagged and kept apart (quarantined) and reported, not used
File the certificates with the job records

ul: Before a plate or length is cut, copy its heat number onto **every** part marked out on it, including the usable offcut, with a paint marker or a low-stress stamp as the specification allows.
Keep a **traceability record**: each part mark against its heat number and certificate.
During welding, the weld record adds the welder's identification and the consumable batch number.
At handover, the job file links every part to its certificate, its welds and its inspection. This is how you can answer a question about the steel years later.

blocks.note: An offcut without a heat number cannot be used on a traceable job. Mark it before you cut, not after.
blocks.label: Tip

ul: Read a class like this: the first number × 100 is the tensile strength in MPa; the first number × the second number × 10 is the yield strength in MPa (8 × 8 × 10 = 640).

The class is stamped on the bolt head. The **nut** has its own class (for example 8 or 10) and must match the bolt: class 8 nuts for 8.8 bolts, class 10 nuts for 10.9 bolts, unless the specification says otherwise.
Imported American bolts may be marked with lines on the head instead: three lines for SAE grade 5, six lines for grade 8.

Never use a lower class, mix classes in one connection, or re-use high-strength bolts that have already been fully tightened unless the specification allows it. Use the washers the specification gives.

blocks.h: Tightening to a manual or specification value

blocks.p: When a manual or specification gives a **torque** (in N·m), use a torque wrench that is in calibration, set to that value. Too little torque lets parts work loose; too much can stretch, strip or snap the bolt. Check whether the figure is for dry or lubricated threads, tighten in the order the manual shows (often a criss-cross pattern), and mark each bolt once it is tightened so that none is missed.
Electrodes and wires are named by a classification, often the American (AWS) one. The classification, not the brand, is what the WPS and specification call for.

head: Classification
Process
What it tells you
rows: E = electrode; 70 = minimum tensile strength 70 ksi (about 480 MPa); 1 = all positions; 8 = low-hydrogen (basic) coating with iron powder, AC or DC+
60 ksi (about 414 MPa); all positions; rutile coating; AC or DC
Solid wire for MIG/MAG (GMAW), also used as a TIG filler rod
ER = electrode or rod; 70 ksi; S = solid; 6 = more manganese and silicon to clean (deoxidise) the weld, good on steel with some mill scale
E = electrode; 7 = 70 ksi; 1 = all positions (0 would mean flat and horizontal only); T = tubular, flux-cored; 1 = its type; C = carbon dioxide (CO₂) shielding gas, M = mixed argon and CO₂
For 304 and 304L stainless; L = low carbon

ul: Solid wire and flux-cored wire belong to different processes (GMAW and FCAW). Swapping one for the other changes the process, so it needs a WPS for the new process.
A change of classification is an essential variable in most codes (see below), even when the size and the reel look the same.
Keep the consumable **batch number** from the packet when the job needs traceability.

blocks.p: The data sheet gives the current or wire-feed and voltage ranges, polarity, shielding gas and flow, positions, typical weld properties, and the **storage and handling** rules.

ul: Low-hydrogen electrodes such as E7018 pick up moisture from the air. Moisture in the coating puts **hydrogen** into the weld, which can cause cracking hours or days later, especially in thick or higher-strength steel.

The data sheet gives the holding-oven temperature, how long electrodes may stay out of the oven, how to re-dry them and how many times re-drying is allowed. A common out-of-oven limit for E7018 under the AWS structural code is about 4 hours, but always use the figure in the data sheet and specification for the job.
Jamaica's humid air makes these limits matter: electrodes left on a bench by an open roller door in the rainy season soak up moisture quickly.

head: Document
What it is
rows: Written instructions for making a weld: process, parent metal and thickness range, joint design, consumables, shielding gas, current, voltage and travel speed ranges, polarity, positions, preheat and interpass temperature, technique, cleaning and any heat treatment
The record of the test weld made to prove the procedure: the actual settings used and the test results (for example bend, tensile, macro and impact tests), signed by the inspector
Proof that a named welder passed a test: process, positions, thickness and diameter range, consumable group. It must be kept up to date

blocks.p: **Essential variables** are the main values in a procedure that affect the properties of the weld. If one of them changes beyond the limits the code allows, the procedure must be qualified again with a new test. The code the job uses gives the full list; typical essential variables are:

ul: The welding process (for example MMAW to FCAW or GMAW)
The parent metal grade or group
The consumable classification
Thickness or diameter outside the qualified range
The shielding gas
The type of current or the polarity
A preheat lower than the one qualified
Adding or leaving out post-weld heat treatment

blocks.note: If you are not sure whether a change is essential, treat it as essential and ask the welding engineer or inspector before welding.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: A welder may weld only within the limits on his or her qualification record: the process, the positions, the thickness and diameter range and the consumable group. Positions use the AWS names:

head: Position
Meaning
rows: Groove (butt) welds in plate: flat, horizontal, vertical, overhead
Fillet welds: flat, horizontal, vertical, overhead
Pipe fixed with its axis horizontal; the welder goes round it (flat, vertical and overhead)
Pipe fixed with its axis at 45°; covers all positions

ul: A qualification usually stays valid only while the welder keeps using the process. Under the AWS codes, a welder who has not used the process for **six months** needs to be tested again. The welder's continuity record proves the process has been used.
Give each weld to a welder qualified for it. Skill and good intentions do not replace the record, and practising on the job itself is not allowed.

blocks.p: Preheat slows the cooling of the weld and lets hydrogen escape, which lowers the risk of cracking. A WPS or preheat table usually asks for **more preheat** when:

ul: The plate is **thicker** (thick plate draws heat away faster)
The steel's **carbon equivalent (CE)** is higher (it hardens more easily)
The joint is heavily restrained
The consumable is not low-hydrogen

blocks.p: The carbon equivalent is worked out from the mill certificate. A common formula is: **CE = C + Mn/6 + (Cr + Mo + V)/5 + (Ni + Cu)/15**. For example, a steel with 0.18% carbon and 1.40% manganese, and very little of the others, has a CE of about 0.18 + 0.23 = 0.41.

ul: Measure preheat with temperature-indicating crayons or a contact thermometer, at the distance from the joint the WPS gives (often about 75 mm), on the side away from the heat source.
A plate that feels hot from the sun is not "preheated": measure it. If it is below the figure in the table, heat it.
Keep to the maximum interpass temperature if the WPS gives one.

blocks.p: **Acceptance criteria** are the limits a weld or item must meet. A good specification gives them as **numbers**, such as "undercut not deeper than 0.5 mm", so that any two inspectors who measure the same weld reach the same decision.

blocks.h: An example of visual acceptance limits

head: Feature
Example limit (your specification gives the real figures)
rows: Not less than the size on the drawing
No single pore larger than 2 mm; no more than a set number in any 100 mm
Overlap, lack of fusion, open craters
Not higher than a set figure (for example 3 mm), blending smoothly into the plate

ul: Have the current specification and drawing, good light, a magnifier and gauges in good condition and in calibration.
Clean the welds of slag and spatter first, so that defects can be seen.
Check in the same order every time. Look for cracks first: any crack is a reject.
Measure each feature at its worst point and compare it with the limit. A reading on the limit passes; any amount beyond it fails.
Mark rejected lengths clearly on the part and keep rejected items apart.
Repair only by an approved method, then inspect again. Grinding a defect so it cannot be seen is not a repair.
Record every reading, with its units, against the weld or item number.

head: Tool
What it measures
rows: Leg length, and throat on convex and concave fillets
Undercut depth, misalignment (high-low), reinforcement height, fillet leg and throat, bevel angle
Fine cracks, pores and the edges of undercut
Lengths, spacing, plate thickness, hole sizes and gaps

head: Method
What it finds
Limits
rows: Only what can be seen; always done first
Cracks and pores **open to the surface**
Works on most non-porous materials, including stainless steel and aluminium; cannot find flaws below the surface
Cracks **at or just below** the surface
Only on magnetic (ferritic) steel; not on aluminium or ordinary (austenitic) stainless steel
Flaws **inside** the weld, especially cracks and lack of fusion; also measures thickness
Needs a skilled, certified operator; difficult on thin or coarse-grained material
Flaws inside the weld, especially porosity and slag; gives a permanent image
Radiation hazard: the area must be cleared; less good at finding cracks lying the wrong way

ul: NDT is done by people certified for the method. The fabricator's job is to make the welds ready and accessible and to record which welds were tested.
When a specification asks for a percentage of welds to be tested, **round up**: 10% of 35 welds is 3.5, so at least 4 welds are tested. The inspector, not the welder, picks which ones.
If a sampled weld fails, the specification usually asks for more welds to be tested. Read what it says.

blocks.p: A good record lets someone else check your work later. It shows: the job and drawing with revisions; each item and weld number; the location; what was checked; each reading with units; the limit; accept or reject; the gauge used; the inspector's name, signature and date. Rejects are raised for repair on a non-conformance report.

blocks.h: What is in a maker's manual

head: Section
What you use it for
rows: Hazards and precautions for this machine. Read it first
Supply, output, duty cycle, weights and sizes, protection rating
Supply voltage, fuse or breaker rating, cable size, earthing, siting and cooling space, generator size
What each control does; how to set up for each process
Tasks the user may do, and how often (daily, weekly, six-monthly); tasks for a technician only
A chart of faults, likely causes and remedies
How the electrical circuits are connected, for the electrician or technician
Each part's name and number, and how the parts fit together
What the maker covers and what voids the cover (often misuse or unauthorised repair)

blocks.h: Reading a welding machine's rating plate

blocks.p: Welding power sources carry a rating plate laid out to the international standard for arc welding equipment (IEC 60974-1). An example for a small inverter MIG set:

head: Symbol
Meaning
Example
rows: Largest current drawn from the supply
Largest effective supply current, used with I₁max to size the supply cable and protection
No-load (open-circuit) voltage: the voltage at the torch or electrode when no arc is struck
Duty cycle: the percentage of a 10-minute period the machine can weld at that current (at 40 °C)
Welding current at each duty cycle
Conventional load voltage at that current
Degree of protection against solid objects and water
S (the letter, often in a box)
Suitable for use where there is an increased risk of electric shock

ul: With the example plate, the machine can weld at 140 A for 6 minutes in every 10. At any current **at or below** the 100% figure (110 A) it can weld without stopping. At a current between two figures, it can weld for at least as long as the higher-current figure allows.
Duty cycles are rated at 40 °C. In a hot workshop, with the machine in the sun or its vents blocked, it will cut out sooner.
U₀ matters for safety: it is present whenever the machine is on, even with no arc.

head: First digit (solids)
Second digit (water)
rows: 2: fingers and objects over 12.5 mm kept out
3: spraying water up to 60° from vertical
4: splashing from any direction; 5: water jets

blocks.note: An IP23 machine is **not** waterproof. Its manual will say it may be stored outside but must not be used in rain unless it is sheltered. On site in the rainy season, plan a shelter for the machine and the work, or work on dry days.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: A **qualified electrician** connects the machine to the supply, using the voltage, current, breaker and cable figures from the manual and rating plate, and checks the earth. Team leaders and trainees do not.
Jamaica's supply is 110 V and 220 V at 50 Hz. Check that the machine is rated for the voltage and for 50 Hz before it is connected.
Site the machine as the manual says: with space round it for cooling air, out of rain and dust, on a firm, level base.
If the machine is to run from a generator, use one of at least the size (kVA) the manual gives. A generator that is too small makes the arc unstable and can damage the electronics in an inverter.

blocks.p: Turn the manual's maintenance table into a **signed checklist** kept with the machine, and check it every week. For a MIG machine this might include:

head: How often
Typical user tasks (follow your manual)
rows: Check cables, torch and plugs for damage; clean spatter from the nozzle; check the contact tip; check the gas hose and regulator; check the cylinder is chained
Clean the drive rolls; blow the liner out with dry air; check drive-roll pressure and the spool brake
With the machine isolated, a competent person removes dust from inside and checks connections; the electrician tests the machine

flow: Stop work and find the chart for the fault you see
Treat each fault separately: two faults may have different causes
Isolate the machine before opening any part the manual allows the user to open
Check the causes in the order the chart gives, simplest first
Change one thing at a time and make a test weld after each change
Leave anything outside the user tasks (for example internal electrical parts) to the technician
Record the fault, the cause found, the parts changed, the test result and who did it

head: MIG fault
Causes a chart usually lists
rows: Worn or wrong-size contact tip; kinked or dirty liner; wrong size or type of drive roll; drive-roll pressure too high or too low; spool brake too tight
Gas cylinder empty or valve closed; flow too low or too high; leaking hose or joint; draughts or fans; spatter in the nozzle; dirty, oily or painted plate; wrong gas
Wire burns back to the tip
Wire speed too low for the voltage; torch held too close; wrong tip size; feed stopping
Voltage and wire speed not matched; poor work-return connection; wrong polarity for the wire

ul: Drive rolls must match the wire: a **V-groove** for solid steel wire, a **U-groove** for soft aluminium wire, a **knurled** groove for flux-cored wire, each in the right size.
The contact tip size must match the wire diameter.
Polarity: solid steel wire and gas-shielded flux-cored wire usually run on DC electrode positive; many self-shielded flux-cored wires run on DC electrode negative. The data sheet decides.

blocks.p: An exploded view shows the parts drawn apart, in the order they fit, each numbered to the parts list. Order by the part number for your exact model and size. If you find a mistake in a manual, such as a wrong part number, record it, tell the supervisor and report it to the supplier; do not just cross it out.

blocks.h: Writing a work instruction from a manual

blocks.p: Give it a title, number and revision, and name the manual it comes from. Say what it covers and who may do the task. List the PPE and safety points first, then numbered steps in plain words, one action per step, with the checks to make. Check every step against the manual, try it with a trainee, then have it approved and dated.

blocks.note: Following the maker's manual is not about who knows best. The maker tested the method, and safe use, the warranty and often the insurance depend on it. When the manual and the Centre's rule differ, the stricter one applies.
blocks.label: Remember

sections.title: Data sheets, safety data sheets and labels

head: Term
Meaning
rows: The percentage of the wet paint that stays on the steel as dry film; the rest evaporates
The thickness of the dried coat, in micrometres (µm). The specification gives it for each coat
The thickness to apply wet, checked with a wet film comb as you paint
How much base and hardener to mix for a two-pack paint
Some two-pack paints must stand for a set time after mixing before use
How long mixed two-pack paint can be used before it starts to set. It is shorter in hot weather
Touch dry, hard dry, full cure
Stages of drying; handling and service depend on them
The minimum time before the next coat, and often a maximum. After the maximum, the surface usually needs abrading or special cleaning before the next coat will stick
The area one litre covers at the given DFT. The practical rate is lower because of losses
Limits for steel temperature, air temperature, relative humidity and the gap above the dew point

blocks.h: Working out film thickness and quantity

ul: **Wet film = dry film × 100 ÷ volume solids %.** Example: a primer with 64% volume solids and a specified DFT of 80 µm needs 80 × 100 ÷ 64 = **125 µm** wet.
**Theoretical spreading rate (m² per litre) = volume solids % × 10 ÷ DFT (µm).** For the same primer: 64 × 10 ÷ 80 = 8 m²/L.
To paint 120 m² at 8 m²/L you need 15 L in theory. Allowing 25% for losses (overspray, uneven steel), you need 15 ÷ 0.75 = **20 L**.

head: Grade (ISO 8501-1)
Description
American (SSPC) equivalent
rows: Blast cleaning to visually clean steel ("white metal")

blocks.p: The **dew point** is the temperature at which water condenses out of the air. If the steel is at or near the dew point, a film of water too thin to see forms on it and the paint will not stick. Most data sheets say: **steel at least 3 °C above the dew point**, and relative humidity not above a set figure (often 85%).

ul: Measure air temperature and relative humidity with a hygrometer, work out the dew point (from a chart or the instrument), and measure the steel temperature with a surface thermometer.
Example: air at 30 °C and 80% relative humidity has a dew point of about 26 °C, so the steel must be at least 29 °C before painting.
Record the readings and the time on the painting record.

blocks.note: In Jamaica, morning dew, afternoon showers and salt air near the coast make these checks essential. Blast-cleaned steel starts to rust (flash rust) within hours in humid air, so it is primed the same day, often within a few hours. Steel cools quickly after sunset, so late-afternoon coats are at risk of condensation.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: Every hazardous product, such as paint, thinner, degreaser, dye penetrant or anti-spatter spray, comes with an SDS in **16 sections**. Read it before the product is used and keep it where users can reach it.

head: Section
What you find
rows: Product and supplier; the hazards and the label elements
What to do about a spill
Physical and chemical properties, including the **flash point**
Stability, health effects, environment, disposal, transport, regulations and other information

blocks.p: The **flash point** is the lowest temperature at which a liquid gives off enough vapour to catch fire from a spark or flame. A liquid with a flash point below the temperature of your workshop (often 30 °C or more in Jamaica) is giving off flammable vapour right now. Keep it well away from welding, grinding and cutting, use it with good ventilation, and keep the lid on.

head: Pictogram (black symbol in a red diamond)
Hazard
rows: Oxidiser: makes other materials burn more fiercely
Corrosion (liquid eating a hand and a metal bar)
Corrosive to skin, eyes or metal
Acutely toxic (can kill in small amounts)
Health hazard (person with a star on the chest)
Serious long-term health effects, such as cancer or breathing sensitisation

ul: **Grinding and cutting discs:** maximum operating speed (rev/min and m/s), size, bore, type and use (metal or stone), and usually an **expiry date** on the centre ring. Never fit a disc rated below the grinder's no-load speed, and do not use one past its expiry date.
**Gas cylinders:** identify the gas by the **label**, not the colour; colours differ between suppliers and countries.
**Electrode and wire packets:** classification, size, current range, polarity, storage and batch number.
**PPE:** filter shade numbers on lenses, impact marks on safety glasses, the standard the item meets.

blocks.p: Use this checklist to test yourself. If you cannot honestly say "I can" to a line, go back to that section and practise with your instructor.

ul: I can say how a standard, a code, a specification, a drawing, a WPS, a manual, a data sheet and an SDS differ, who writes each and how binding it is.
I can read the scope, normative references, definitions and annexes of a standard, and say why each matters.
I can tell a firm requirement ("shall") from a recommendation ("should") or a permission ("may").
I can apply general and specific tolerances, and convert imperial units safely.
I can check that a document is current against the register and deal with an old copy in use.
I can apply an order of priority, raise and log a written query, and explain a concession.
I can review a specification pack and log the problems I find.
I can read steel grades such as S355J2, a mill certificate and its type, and match steel to certificates by heat number.
I can keep traceability through cutting and welding.
I can read bolt and nut property classes and apply a torque value from a manual.
I can read consumable classifications such as E7018, ER70S-6 and E71T-1C, and follow storage rules from a data sheet.
I can explain a WPS, a PQR, essential variables and welder qualification limits.
I can say why preheat rises with thickness and carbon equivalent, and measure it.
I can inspect welds against numerical acceptance limits with the right gauges and record the results.
I can say what each NDT method finds and where it cannot be used.
I can read a welding machine's rating plate, including duty cycle, U₀ and IP rating.
I can use a manual to install (through an electrician), maintain and fault-find a machine, one change at a time.
I can use a paint data sheet to plan coats, conditions, film thickness and quantity.
I can find the flash point and PPE in an SDS, and read hazard pictograms and product labels.
I can write a short work instruction from a manual and brief my team on a document's requirements.

terms: The limits, usually numerical, that work must meet to be accepted
A figure, worked out from the steel's analysis, that shows how easily it hardens and cracks when welded
Written permission from the client or engineer to accept work or material that does not fully meet the specification
The temperature at which moisture condenses from the air
The thickness of a dried paint coat, in micrometres
The percentage of a 10-minute period a machine can weld at a given current
A procedure value which, if changed, needs a new procedure test
The lowest temperature at which a liquid gives off vapour that can be ignited
The number on steel that links it to its mill certificate
A rating of how well equipment keeps out solids and water
The steel maker's certificate of analysis and test results for a heat of steel
A record of work or material that does not meet a requirement, and what will be done
Another document that must be used with a standard
The voltage at the electrode or torch when no arc is struck
How long mixed two-pack paint can be used before it starts to set
The record of the test weld and results that prove a WPS
The strength marking of a bolt or nut, such as 8.8
The 16-section document giving the hazards and safe use of a product
The amount a size may vary from the size given
Being able to link each part back to its certificate, welds and inspection
The section of a manual listing faults, causes and remedies
The written instructions for making a weld
The thickness of paint applied wet, checked with a comb gauge
The stress at which a metal starts to stretch permanently

c1.title: A stair tower for a hotel in Ocho Rios
c1.text: Shanice leads a team of three building a steel stair tower for a hotel in Ocho Rios, St Ann. The document register lists the general arrangement drawing at revision C, but the copy pinned up in the shop is a revision B photocopy. The specification says: "Fillet welds shall be 6 mm unless a larger size is shown on the drawings" and "Blast-cleaned stringers should be primed within 4 hours." The drawing shows 8 mm fillets on the stringer brackets, carries the general note "Tolerances ±3 mm unless stated", and dimensions the landing beam as 2400 ± 1.

c2.title: Steel for a water-treatment platform in Bog Walk
c2.text: Dwayne is checking a delivery of plate and bolts for a walkway platform at a water-treatment works near Bog Walk, St Catherine. The specification asks for S355J2 steel with EN 10204 type 3.1 certificates, and class 8.8 bolts with class 8 nuts. He finds that one plate's heat number does not appear on any certificate, that the certificate for another heat is type 2.2, that a third certificate shows the grade as S355JR, and that the nuts in the bolt boxes are stamped 5.

c3.title: A warehouse frame in Portmore
c3.text: A shop is fabricating the frame of a warehouse in Portmore, St Catherine. The WPS is for MMAW with E7018 electrodes on S355 steel, and its preheat table asks for 75 °C on plate over 20 mm thick. The base plates are 30 mm. The specification says 10% of the 26 complete-penetration butt welds shall be tested by UT. The supervisor wants to switch to flux-cored wire to speed up. One welder, Kirk, has a qualification record for MMAW, but his continuity record shows he has not used the process for eight months.

c4.title: A new MIG machine at a training centre in Montego Bay
c4.text: Andre, a Level 3 trainee at a training centre in Montego Bay, St James, is preparing a new inverter MIG machine. Its rating plate shows: X 25% at 250 A, 60% at 160 A and 100% at 125 A; IP23S. The manual says to run it from a generator of at least 10 kVA. The first job uses 1.2 mm E71T-1C flux-cored wire, but the machine came with 1.0 mm V-groove drive rolls fitted. A site job at a farm is planned, where the only generator is 6.5 kVA.

c5.title: Painting school gates in Mandeville
c5.text: Kerry-Ann is planning the painting of steel gates for a school in Mandeville, Manchester. The specification asks for a primer at 110 µm DFT. The primer's data sheet gives 55% volume solids; overcoat interval 6 hours minimum and 7 days maximum at 25 °C; and "apply only when the steel is at least 3 °C above the dew point and relative humidity is below 85%". One morning she reads: air 24 °C, relative humidity 90%, dew point 22 °C, steel 22 °C. Some gates were primed three weeks ago and have not yet had their finish coat.

questions.q: Shanice notices the revision B photocopy on the shop wall. What should she do first?
o: Let the team finish today's work from B, then swap the copies tomorrow
Write "revision C" on the photocopy so the team knows it is current
Keep using B, since a revision seldom changes anything structural
Stop work that relies on it, get revision C and check what changed
questions.why: Work from a superseded drawing can be wrong in ways nobody sees until it fails inspection. Stop the work that depends on it, get the current revision from the register, and check whether anything already made is affected.

questions.q: What fillet size applies to the stringer brackets?
o: 8 mm: the specification lets the drawing show a larger size
6 mm, because a specification always comes before a drawing
7 mm, as a fair compromise between the two documents
Neither, until the client has issued a new contract
questions.why: Read the exact words: the specification itself says a larger size shown on the drawings applies. There is no conflict to settle here, so the 8 mm on the drawing is the size to weld.

questions.q: A team member says the primer timing is optional because the specification only says "should". What is the best reply?
o: "Should" is the expected way; another needs a reason and approval
He is right: "should" means the team can prime whenever it suits them
"Should" is just as firm as "shall", so it can never be changed by anyone
"Should" applies only if the client is on site to watch the work
questions.why: "Should" is a recommendation: the method to use unless another is agreed for a good reason. In Jamaica's humid air, blasted steel rusts within hours, which is exactly why the recommendation is there.

questions.q: The landing beam measures 2402.5 mm. What is the right decision?
o: Within tolerance: the general note allows 2397 to 2403 mm
Within tolerance: the two tolerances add together to ±4 mm in all
Out of tolerance: its own ±1 gives limits of 2399 to 2401 mm
Out of tolerance only if the client happens to notice it
questions.why: A tolerance written on a particular dimension overrides the general note for that dimension. 2402.5 mm is 1.5 mm over the 2400 mm size, beyond the ±1 allowed, so the beam must be raised as a non-conformance.

questions.q: What should Dwayne do with the plate whose heat number is not on any certificate?
o: Use it on the less important parts of the walkway, where strength matters less
Copy a heat number from one of the other certificates onto it
Tag it, keep it apart and report it until a matching certificate is supplied
Use it, since it arrived on the same truck as the certified plates
questions.why: Without a matching certificate there is no proof of the plate's grade or test results, and traceability is broken. It is quarantined and reported, never used or re-marked.

questions.q: Why is the type 2.2 certificate a problem when the specification asks for type 3.1?
o: It is exactly the same as a 3.1, only printed on a different form
A 2.2 is for stainless steel, so it cannot apply to S355 plate
Its results are routine ones, not tests on the steel supplied
It shows a higher grade, which makes the plate too hard to weld
questions.why: A type 3.1 certificate gives results from tests on the actual product supplied, checked by an inspection department independent of production. A 2.2 does not meet that requirement, so Dwayne asks for a 3.1 or a written concession.

questions.q: What does the certificate showing S355JR tell Dwayne about that heat?
o: It is weaker in yield, at about 275 MPa instead of 355 MPa
It was impact-tested at +20 °C, not at −20 °C as J2 requires
It is the same steel as S355J2, so the letters do not matter
It is a rust-resisting grade that cannot be welded or painted
questions.why: Both grades have a minimum yield of 355 MPa, but the letters give the impact test temperature: JR at +20 °C, J2 at −20 °C. JR does not meet a J2 requirement, so the steel is held and a query raised.

questions.q: What should be done about the nuts stamped 5?
o: Use them, as their thread size is exactly the same as the bolts
Use them, but tighten each one a little harder to make up for it
Hold them back and get class 8 nuts to match the 8.8 bolts
Use them, with a spring washer fitted under each one
questions.why: A nut must be as strong as the bolt; a weaker nut can strip its thread before the bolt reaches its load. The specification calls for class 8 nuts with class 8.8 bolts, so the class 5 nuts are not used.

questions.q: Why can the shop not simply switch from MMAW to flux-cored wire to speed up?
o: Flux-cored wire cannot be used on any grade of structural steel
A change of process needs a WPS qualified for flux-cored welding
The change is allowed if the welders use the same current setting
Only the electrode packet changes, so the existing WPS still covers it
questions.why: The welding process is an essential variable. Changing it means a new WPS, proved by a procedure test, and welders qualified for that process, before any production weld is made.

questions.q: What does Kirk's eight-month gap mean for his work on this frame?
o: Nothing, as a qualification once passed lasts for the whole of a career
He can weld, provided a qualified welder checks his first few joints
He may weld fillet welds but not any of the butt welds
His qualification has lapsed; he must be re-tested before he welds
questions.why: Under the AWS codes a welder who has not used the process for six months must be tested again. The continuity record is the evidence, and here it shows the qualification is no longer in force.

questions.q: At the very least, how many of the frame's complete-penetration joints must go for ultrasonic examination?
questions.why: 10% of 26 is 2.6. You cannot test part of a weld, and testing 2 would be less than 10%, so you round up to 3. The inspector, not the welder, chooses which welds.

questions.q: A welder says the base plates are already hot from the sun, so no preheat is needed. What should happen?
o: Accept it, since steel in the Jamaican sun is always above 75 °C
Skip the preheat and use a slower travel speed instead
Preheat only the last run, when the joint is nearly full
Measure near the joint and heat to at least 75 °C if it is lower
questions.why: Preheat is measured, not guessed. Sun-warmed steel is rarely near 75 °C, and 30 mm plate draws heat away fast. Check with a crayon or thermometer at the distance the WPS gives, and heat if it is below the figure.

questions.q: A trainee will weld long seams at 150 A. What does the rating plate tell Andre?
o: Only 2.5 minutes in every 10, the 25% figure on the plate
Without stopping at all, because 150 A is close to the 100% current
Exactly 5 minutes in every 10, halfway between the two figures
At least 6 minutes in every 10, as 150 A is below the 60% current
questions.why: At 160 A the plate allows 60%, and a lower current always allows a longer time, so 150 A gives at least 6 minutes in every 10. Only at 125 A or less can it weld without stopping. A hot workshop shortens these times.

questions.q: Which drive rolls should be fitted for the first job?
o: Knurled rolls for 1.2 mm wire, with a 1.2 mm contact tip
The fitted 1.0 mm V-groove rolls, with extra drive-roll pressure
U-groove rolls for 1.2 mm wire, as used for soft wire
V-groove rolls for 1.2 mm wire, with a 1.0 mm contact tip
questions.why: Flux-cored wire is soft enough to be crushed in a V-groove, so a knurled groove of the right size is used; U-grooves are for aluminium. The contact tip must match the wire diameter, or the feed will be erratic.

questions.q: What does the "C" at the end of E71T-1C tell Andre to set up?
o: A mixed argon and CO₂ shielding gas
Carbon dioxide (CO₂) shielding gas
No shielding gas, as the flux protects it
Pure argon shielding gas
questions.why: In this classification C means the wire is classified with CO₂ shielding and M means mixed argon and CO₂. The T and 1 show a gas-shielded flux-cored wire, so it does need gas.

questions.q: What should Andre plan for the site job at the farm?
o: Get a generator of at least 10 kVA, as the manual says
Use the 6.5 kVA generator and keep the welding current low
Use the 6.5 kVA generator and weld only in short bursts
Run the machine off the farmhouse lighting circuit
questions.why: A generator smaller than the manual gives makes the arc unstable and can damage an inverter's electronics. Turning the current down does not make the supply right; get a generator of the size the maker states.

questions.q: What wet film thickness should the painters apply for the primer?
o: 60 µm
110 µm
165 µm
200 µm
questions.why: Wet film = dry film × 100 ÷ volume solids % = 110 × 100 ÷ 55 = 200 µm. Only 55% of the wet paint stays as dry film, so the wet coat must be thicker than the dry figure.

questions.q: From Kerry-Ann's morning readings, what should she decide?
o: Paint now, because the air at 24 °C is warmer than the dew point
Wait until the steel is 25 °C and humidity is under 85%
Paint now, but add extra thinner so that the paint dries faster
Paint now and apply a thicker coat to make up for the damp
questions.why: The steel is at the dew point, so a film of water is forming on it, and the humidity is over the limit. The steel must be at least 3 °C above the 22 °C dew point (25 °C) and the humidity below 85% before painting.

questions.q: What should be done before the finish coat goes on the gates primed three weeks ago?
o: Prepare the surface as the data sheet says for a late overcoat
Nothing, since an older primer is harder and holds paint better
Apply a second coat of primer over it without any preparation
Strip all the primer off and blast the gates back to bare metal
questions.why: The maximum overcoat interval has passed, so the next coat may not bond. Data sheets usually ask for the surface to be cleaned and abraded, or give another method; follow it rather than painting straight over or stripping everything.

questions.q: A standard's normative references list another standard with a year after its number. Which edition of that standard must be used?
o: The latest edition, whatever year is shown
Any edition the team happens to have in the shop
The edition of that year, even if a newer one exists
None, as normative references are only reading lists
questions.why: A dated reference means that edition only; an undated reference means the latest edition. Normative references are requirements, unlike the bibliography, which is only further reading.
